text:
The last part of each lesson is the "Evaluate" section.

Science and engineering aren't about figuring everything out all at once, it's about making incremental progress: making smaller improvements over time to design a big project that actually works.

After you develop something, you'll spend some time evaluating it: What worked? What didn't? Why? What are your next steps?

Evaluate your design: what is good about it?

What could be improved?

tiles.title: What is good about your design?

text:
Collaboration is a major parts of engineering: engineers work in teams, and often share ideas to get feedback from other teams.

That's what we will do now!

Demo at your table

One or two group members will demonstrate the prototype.

Make sure you explain:

  1. Who you are designing for
  2. What motion you are trying to make the prosthesis do
  3. Why you think that motion will be helpful for that person.

Make sure you take notes, and remind the people visiting to leave their comments!

As you talk about your prototype, try to think: what are important characteristics of a prosthesis? What about of any type of prototype?

Walking around the class

The rest of your group: Walk around the class and look at other people's prototypes.

Ask them questions, and give them constructive feedback!

  • What did they do that you didn't think of?
  • What could be improved in their design?
  • Does their design seem like it would help the person they are designing for? If not, what could be changed?
  • What did your group make that they could learn from?

As you see other prototypes, try to think: what are important characteristics of a prosthesis prototype?

tiles.title: Figuring out what makes good prototypes

text:
Now that you have seen a lot of different prototypes, write down some characteristics of good prosthetic hands or arms.

You might not always be working on prostheses, so after that, think about characteristics of good prototypes in general.
